source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33
finding: Behavioral science samples come from a thin slice of humanity, yet papers draw claims about the human mind. This is the core confound in East-West reasoning work: one population is the default, the other is the 'different' group.
numbers: Arnett's count of top journals 2003-2007: 68% of subjects from the US, 96% from Western industrialized countries (countries with 12% of world population). 73% of first authors at US universities, 99% at Western universities.
limits: A narrative review, not a meta-analysis. Authors say critics may charge cherry-picking. Sample counts are for 2003-2007 journals only.
agent_relevance: Evidence weighting: a finding tested on one culture's students is a claim about that group, not about 'thinking'. Our agent should tag each human-evidence line with the population tested.

source: Segall, Campbell, Herskovits (1966) The influence of culture on visual perception, as reported in Henrich et al. 2010
finding: Mueller-Lyer illusion strength varies across 16 societies (14 small-scale). Even a 'hard-wired' perceptual effect depends on the visual world a person grew up in. US undergraduates were at the extreme; San foragers showed no effect.
numbers: US undergraduates needed line 'a' about one fifth longer than line 'b' to see them as equal (PSE). San foragers of the Kalahari: PSE not distinguishable from zero. Variation also found for Sander parallelogram and horizontal-vertical illusions. Read only through Henrich 2010, not the original book.
limits: Original data from the 1960s; the explanation (carpentered-world exposure) is debated. Numbers come from the secondary text.
agent_relevance: Even low-level processes are not safe universals. A claim that reasoning is universal needs diverse samples, not just a plausible mechanism.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33 (section 4: reasoning and categorization)
finding: Review of analytic vs holistic evidence: attention, categorization, deductive reasoning and attribution all vary by population in predictable ways. Authors state both styles are available to all normal adults; what differs is habitual use. Some effects reverse, not just shrink.
numbers: Americans group by deterministic rule; East Asians group by family resemblance (Norenzayan et al. 2002b). Same stimuli in Turkish Black Sea herders, fishers and farmers (Uskul 2008): European-Americans were most rule-based and outliers by absolute distance from zero. Mapuche (Chile) and Sangu (Tanzania) farmers resembled the Chinese pattern, exaggerated toward holistic.
quote: although analytic and holistic cognitive systems are available to all normal adults
limits: Authors note Westerners are not unique in style, only at the end of the distribution. Relies on others' data; no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Supports 'universal capacity, variable default'. Our schema should treat holistic and analytic modes as both available, chosen by cue, not as two kinds of minds.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33 (section 4: attention and context)
finding: Field-dependence and context sensitivity: Westerners and migratory foragers sit at the field-independent end; East Asians, Malays, Russians more field-dependent. Self-construal primes shift processing within a person.
numbers: Canadians less field-dependent than Chinese, who were less than Arabs (Norenzayan 2007). Within-country contrasts (northern vs southern Italy, Hokkaido vs mainland Japan, west vs east Europe) differ in holistic processing (Varnum 2008). Independent primes foster analytic processing and interdependent primes foster holistic (Oyserman & Lee 2008).
limits: Priming evidence is subject to replication worries (see the priming-of-orientation subfield). Rod and Frame results come from many labs with uneven sample sizes.
agent_relevance: Orientation can be shifted by context cues. This is the human version of prompt-induced style shifts in an LLM.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33 (open peer commentary on task interpretation)
finding: A commentary in the same issue argues that apparent cultural differences can reflect how people interpret the task, not different processes. Same experiment, different understood situation.
numbers: Example for economic games: participants may bring fairness rules about who produced the money, friendship or rights, so offers differ because the scenario differs. The commentators propose giving all groups the same rich context to test this.
limits: A commentary, argued from reasoning, not a new data set.
agent_relevance: For LLM tests: a different answer in two languages may reflect a different pragmatic reading of the prompt. Control by matching context and instruction.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33 (open peer commentary on Luria and early cross-cultural work)
finding: Commentary recalls that Luria (1930s Uzbekistan), Cole, Greenfield, Dasen and Lancy found different reasoning patterns tied to schooling and institutions, not a fixed developmental sequence. Cognitive 'development' tracked exposure to modern institutions.
numbers: Piagetian tasks tested in West Africa and Papua New Guinea 'didn't hold up very well, especially beyond early childhood'. Kohlberg post-conventional reasoning: Snarey (1985) meta-analysis of 27 countries found it in all Western urban samples and in no small-scale society.
limits: Secondary summary of old, often contested work (test familiarity, how syllogism tasks are read). No effect sizes given.
agent_relevance: Schooling and task familiarity are a confound of 'culture'. The agent should discount contrasts where one group knows the task format better.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition. Psych Review 108
finding: The founding theory: East Asian social worlds (interdependence, complexity) lead to holistic thought (context attention, relationships, cyclic change, tolerance of contradiction). Western social worlds lead to analytic thought (objects, categories, rules, linear change, non-contradiction).
numbers: Not opened. Described by Jin et al. 2023 and Henrich et al. 2010. No numbers recorded.
limits: Known only through secondary text. Treat details as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: This is the theory the 'critiques and universals' subfield tests. Treat it as one hypothesis about default style, not proof of different reasoning engines.

source: Norenzayan, Smith, Kim, Nisbett (2002) Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning. Cognitive Science 26
finding: Core paradigm for rule vs similarity: categorise a new item by a deterministic rule (formal) or by family resemblance (intuitive). European-Americans lean to rule; Asian-Americans in between; East Asians lean to resemblance.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not read. Direction only, from Henrich Fig. 5: European-American students most rule-based, East Asian students least.
limits: Not opened. College students in a lab; the groups differ in language, schooling and test familiarity.
agent_relevance: The rule-vs-similarity split maps to our operators: code-checked rules vs analogy. The agent should pick by task type, not by 'culture'.

source: Masuda & Nisbett (2001) Attending holistically versus analytically: comparing the context sensitivity of Japanese and Americans. JPSP 81
finding: Fish-scene paradigm: Japanese described and recalled more background and relations; Americans focused on the focal fish. Recall of objects is worse for East Asians when the background is switched.
numbers: Not opened; direction only, via Henrich 2010 ('East Asians' recall for objects is worse than Americans' if the background has been switched').
limits: Replication status not checked this session. Effect sizes unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Context sensitivity is a testable claim. An agent should check what is background and what is focal before reasoning.

source: Peng & Nisbett (1999) Culture, dialectics, and reasoning about contradiction. American Psychologist 54
finding: Chinese participants preferred dialectical proverbs and compromise resolutions of contradiction; Americans preferred formal logic and one-sided resolutions.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Proverb preference is a weak proxy for reasoning, and translated wording is a confound.
agent_relevance: Contradiction tolerance is a style, not a deficit. Rule G1 (doubt on signal) should not penalise holding two models open when evidence is mixed.

source: Blais, Jack, Scheepers, Fiset, Caldara (2008) Culture shapes how we look at faces. PLoS ONE 3
finding: A 'universal' face-scanning pattern (triangle over eyes and mouth) was not universal. East Asian observers fixated the centre of the face more, across learning, recognition and race-categorization tasks.
numbers: 14 Western Caucasian and 14 East Asian adults (mean ages 24.4 and 23.2). East Asians were new international students in Glasgow. Same-race recognition advantage in both groups (p<.01 Westerners, p<.04 East Asians). No main effect of culture on accuracy (F(1,26)=0.59, p=.44).
limits: Small N. Accuracy was equal between groups, so strategy differed while performance did not. Authors link it to holistic strategy; gaze-avoidance norms are another reading.
agent_relevance: Different process, same accuracy: different traces do not mean different quality. Do not rank styles by how they look.

source: Caldara, Zhou, Miellet (2010) Putting culture under the 'spotlight' reveals universal information use for face recognition. PLoS ONE 5
finding: Follow-up from the same group: when the visible window is forced small (gaze-contingent spotlight), Western and East Asian observers use the same information (eyes and part of the mouth). The cultural gap in eye movements disappears. Cultural strategy shows up only when viewing is free.
numbers: 30 Western Caucasian and 30 East Asian (Chinese) observers; spotlight of 2, 5 and 8 degrees. No culture x aperture interaction in accuracy (F(2,54)=0.6, p=.55) or response time (F(2,54)=0.58, p=.56). Groups equally accurate (F(1,54)=2.18, p=.14). At 8 degrees East Asians again fixated the nose.
quote: Westerners and Easterners observers rely on the very same information to recognize faces
limits: Face recognition, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Best model of 'universal capacity, culturally set default'. Constrain the situation and style differences vanish. Constrained, code-checked steps in our schema should do the same for an LLM.

source: Talhelm, Zhang, Oishi (2018) Moving chairs in Starbucks: observational studies find rice-wheat cultural differences in daily life in China. Science Advances 4
finding: Within-China contrast (rice south vs wheat north) that avoids the East-vs-West language and nationality confound. Wheat-region people sat alone more and moved a blocking chair rather than squeeze past.
numbers: Study 1: 8,964 people counted in cafes in six cities (Beijing, Shenyang = wheat; Shanghai, Nanjing, Guangzhou, Hong Kong = rice). About 10% more alone in wheat area on weekdays, about 5% more on weekends. Study 2: chair moved to block aisle, n = 678. Cities chosen with >70% rice or <20% rice farmland.
limits: Observational, six big cities, not randomised. Region is still confounded with climate, dialect, income, history. Tests social orientation, not analytic-holistic reasoning directly.
agent_relevance: Useful design pattern: compare groups that share language and nation to strip confounds. Prefer evidence from such matched designs.

source: Jin et al. (2023) The cultural psychology of large language models: is ChatGPT a holistic or analytic thinker? arXiv 2308.14242
finding: First test of Nisbett-style scales on ChatGPT. On cognitive-process measures GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 scored more holistic than human norms; on value measures they did not lean East.
numbers: Analysis-Holism Scale: GPT-3.5 M=5.35 (SD 0.11), GPT-4 M=5.01 (SD 0.10), norm 4.87 (SD 0.49, N=702), both p<.001, n=10 runs each. Dialectical Self Scale: GPT-3.5 4.59 vs norm 4.00 (N=158, p<.001); GPT-4 3.97 (p=.344). Independent self-construal: GPT-3.5 6.98, GPT-4 5.32 vs norm 4.73 (N=382, both p<.001). Interdependent: GPT-3.5 5.85 vs 4.81 (p<.001); GPT-4 4.95 (p=.07). Triadic categorisation relational share: GPT-3.5 0.87, GPT-4 0.85.
limits: Only n=10 runs per cell at temperature 1; self-report scales that agree-bias inflates; two OpenAI models; no human comparison on the same items. Mixed results inside the one paper.
agent_relevance: Self-report scales on an LLM measure agreeableness and wording, not thinking style. Do not use them to pick a reasoning mode.

source: Sun & Wang (2025) The fragility of 'cultural tendencies' in LLMs. arXiv 2510.05869
finding: Failed conceptual replication of Lu, Song, Zhang (Nature Human Behaviour): prompt language (English vs Chinese) and model origin had negligible effect across 8 LLMs. Original items and templates were withheld, so the replication was conceptual.
numbers: 8 models (gpt-4.1, gemini-2.5, claude-sonnet-4, grok-4 and Chinese models incl. ernie, deepseek, qwen), 4 experiments, temperature 0. Exp 1 (960 observations): language effect d=0.045, eta2=0.0002, p=.15; model origin d=0.169, p=.0089; framing d=-2.095, eta2=0.542. Exp 2: language significant in 3 of 8 models (ernie d=-0.171, qwen d=0.540, gpt d=-0.190). McNemar tests on bilingual models: no language effect (all p>0.1); agreement 86.7-93.3%.
limits: Own materials, not LSZ's; temperature 0 and forced reasoning differ from the original. Effect for qwen is not zero. Single preprint.
agent_relevance: Prompt framing (change-framed vs neutral) moved scores about 20 times more than prompt language by d. Use framing carefully, and do not expect language to switch reasoning style.

source: Hu, Peng, Zhao, Qiu, Hung, Peng (2026) Machine Culture: emergent phenomenon in LLMs. arXiv 2601.17096
finding: 2x2 design (US vs Chinese model x English vs Chinese prompt) over eight tasks. Model origin did not predict 'holistic' traits and prompt language did not cause stable frame-switching. 'Cultural reversal': English prompts gave more East-Asian-like outputs than Chinese prompts in some tasks.
numbers: 100 runs per condition per task (400 per task), temperature 1. Scene task object counts: English 10.91 vs Chinese 10.07 (p<.001). Categorisation relational score for the Chinese model: Chinese prompt 5.30 vs English 6.78 (t=-7.74, p<.001), opposite to bilingual human evidence.
limits: Preprint by authors from the Nisbett lineage; ERNIE is the only Chinese model I confirmed; item-level materials not checked.
agent_relevance: Supports a null on 'culture by language' for LLMs. RLHF seems to flatten style variance, so style is not a free control knob.

source: Tao, Viberg, Baker, Kizilcec (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of large language models. PNAS Nexus 3
finding: Five GPT versions answered World Values Survey items. Outputs resembled English-speaking and Protestant European countries. Cultural prompting (naming a country) helped later models.
numbers: Models: GPT-3, 3.5-turbo, 4, 4-turbo, 4o. Cultural prompting improved alignment for 71-81% of countries and territories in GPT-4, 4-turbo, 4o. GPT-4o closest to Finland (d=0.20), Andorra (0.21); farthest Jordan (4.10), Libya (4.00). GPT-4 closest to New Zealand (0.98), farthest Jordan (4.19).
limits: Values survey, not reasoning. Survey answers need not predict behaviour in use (authors' own caveat). Only OpenAI models.
agent_relevance: Default LLM output sits at the WEIRD end, matching the Henrich critique. A short explicit cue shifts the default, so state the framing the task needs rather than leaving it implied.

source: Cao, Zhou, Lee, Cabello, Chen, Hershcovich (2023) Assessing cross-cultural alignment between ChatGPT and human societies. arXiv 2303.17466
finding: With US framing ChatGPT aligned strongly with American Hofstede scores but adapted poorly to other cultures. English prompts compressed variance and pulled answers toward American culture.
numbers: Spearman correlations with human survey: US 0.70 (p=.12) on prompt 1; China -0.77 (p=.07) on prompt 1 and +0.54 (p=.27) on prompt 2; Spain 0.93 (p=.01) on combined prompts 1&2. Adding a correct cultural description raised a 1-5 alignment score from 1.5 to 2.5; an incorrect description lowered it to 1.0.
limits: Very few data points per country so p-values are weak; ChatGPT March 2023 version; sign flips across prompts show instability.
agent_relevance: Instability across prompt wording is itself the finding: the same model gives correlations of opposite sign. Always run several wordings and report spread.

source: Cultural dominance of English in LLMs benchmark (arXiv 2310.12481)
finding: Non-English queries to GPT models still returned English-culture answers; GPT-4 was most affected, text-davinci-003 least.
numbers: Benchmark of concrete objects (holidays, songs) and abstract objects (values and opinions from multilingual public opinion surveys) across eight languages. For ChatGPT the share of answers tied to English culture exceeded the share tied to the queried culture. Exact percentages not recorded.
limits: I read the abstract, first page and a results sentence; author names and exact title not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Strengthens the null for language as a culture switch: the prompt language does not remove English-centred defaults.

source: AlKhamissi et al. (2024) Investigating cultural alignment of large language models. arXiv 2402.13231
finding: Simulated Egyptian and US surveys with real respondent personas. Alignment is higher when prompted in the culture's dominant language and when pretraining has a better language mix. Misalignment is worse for underrepresented personas and sensitive topics. 'Anthropological prompting' helps.
numbers: Abstract-level reading only in this session; no per-condition numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract only. Egypt and US only. Survey personas, not reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Language can matter for values when pretraining data supports it. This cuts against the pure-null reading of Sun & Wang; the disagreement is a boundary condition to test.

source: Atari, Xue, Park, Blasi, Henrich (2023) Which humans? PsyArXiv
finding: Argues that LLM outputs on psychological measures sit closest to WEIRD populations and that similarity falls with cultural distance from the US.
numbers: Not opened: the cached page I fetched held only a reference list (6,933 characters). Finding known from a search snippet only; no numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified in this session.
agent_relevance: Reference point for the claim that LLMs inherit WEIRD defaults. Read the full paper before citing any number.

source: Appraisal of Jin et al. 2023 design (own reading)
finding: Confounds in the LLM tests: mixed results inside one paper (holistic on process scales, not on value scales), only 10 runs per condition, self-report scales with no behavioral ground truth for a model, and human norms from different populations. The same scale cannot tell whether the model 'thinks' holistically.
numbers: AHS norm N=702, DSS norm N=158, SCS norm N=382, versus 10 LLM runs per model. Triadic task had no human norm in the paper; compared with provincial Chinese means from other work.
limits: My own appraisal from the paper text, not a published critique.
agent_relevance: Evidence weighting rule: LLM scale scores with n<=10 and no behavioral check get low weight.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33 (authors' reply on artifacts and cherry-picking)
finding: Authors answer two worries: (a) they cherry-picked extreme cases; (b) differences are artifacts of translating experiments across contexts. They agree much of human psychology is shared and say the aim is to measure similarity and variation, not assume either.
numbers: Not a data paper. They ask that journals require at least two samples or methods for broad claims (their analogy: Nature Genetics requires two independent samples).
limits: Defensive reply by the authors themselves.
agent_relevance: Gives a policy to copy: a claimed universal reasoning rule needs at least two diverse sources before it becomes a guardrail.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world? Behav Brain Sci 33 (economic games contrast)
finding: A cooperation contrast, often cited with the reasoning work: US adults sit at the extreme end of fairness behaviour across 23 small-scale societies.
numbers: Dictator Game mean offer highest in the US adult sample; US offers nearly double those of the Hadza and Tsimane. Industrialized samples usually offer 40-50% in the Ultimatum Game, modal 50%; offers below about 30% are often rejected.
limits: Interpretation disputed (commentary: task meaning differs by group). Not about reasoning.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as the reasoning work: the Western student is the outlier, not the baseline.

source: Cross-paper comparison: Lu et al., Sun & Wang 2025, Hu et al. 2026
finding: Both preprints report weak or reversed language effects, while Lu, Song, Zhang report that Chinese prompts yield more interdependent and holistic output (known to me only from a search summary and Sun & Wang's description). Three studies, three results: the effect depends on model, items, temperature.
numbers: Sun & Wang: language d=0.045 overall (8 models, temperature 0). Hu et al.: 400 observations per task, temperature 1, reversal in categorisation (5.30 vs 6.78). Original LSZ: 100 responses per language per measure and 4-12 items per task over 7 tasks and 2 models (per Sun & Wang).
limits: My synthesis; the LSZ original was not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat LLM 'culture' effects as unstable. Only act on an effect that holds across model families and wordings.

source: Hu et al. 2026 (Service Persona Camouflage)
finding: RLHF-tuned models give hyper-positive, near zero-variance answers on affect tasks, hiding any cultural variance that pretraining may hold. The authors call this mode collapse from safety alignment.
numbers: ERNIE with English prompt: mean 5.00, SD 0.00 on ideal low-arousal positive affect, 100% ceiling rate.
limits: One task family and one model for the extreme case; the RLHF cause is not tested by ablation.
agent_relevance: An aligned model can show less variation than any human group. Sample variance is a weak signal of 'many views' in our agent.

source: Sun & Wang (2025) (methodological critique of the original LSZ study)
finding: Three concerns about LLM cultural-psychology work: anthropomorphism (human scales on LLMs), unclear cause (training data, tokenization, language structure), and lack of transparency (items, templates withheld). Also too few items (4-12 per task) and only two models.
numbers: Their replication: 8 models; framing explained eta2=0.542 of variance in Exp 1, language 0.0002.
limits: Critics' view; the original authors' reply was not read.
agent_relevance: Log whether items and prompts were released. No materials means low weight.
